assessment.nobel_worthiness: The IceCube detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos, followed by the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations, opened neutrino astronomy and gave a direct handle on cosmic-ray accelerators. It required a genuinely new instrument, a cubic-kilometre Cherenkov array in Antarctic ice, which I value as an experimentalist in astroparticle physics.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the project and Karle was central to the construction and the detector and calibration work. The credited pair is a coherent, compact allocation; the very large collaboration and earlier pioneers (AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND) complicate the story a little. I have not independently verified who held which role.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed in several channels and the source associations are strengthening. The astrophysical origin of most of the flux is still unresolved, but the discovery itself is solid and the timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Origin of the bulk of the diffuse flux remains unsettled
Credit relative to AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers and to the wider collaboration

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with magic-wavelength trapping, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and underpins redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and searches for new physics. It is an original idea turned into an instrument of exceptional performance with a clear lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye drove its realisation to the highest precision. The two-person allocation looks fair. Other contributors to Sr and Yb lattice clocks, and the earlier single-ion clock work already recognised in 2012, mean a careful statement of the contribution is needed.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many laboratories with international comparisons, and mature enough that the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Boundary with the 2012 and 2005 prizes in precision spectroscopy must be argued
Which clock species and groups deserve mention in the citation

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC by two independent detectors completed the Standard Model's particle content and is among the most consequential experimental results in the field. It is also a triumph of detector design, trigger and calorimeter instrumentation, which is close to my own experience in collaborations.
assessment.attribution: The prize rules and the one-to-three limit make this the hardest attribution on the list. I would favour the proposers and leaders of the experiments, but any selection among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee excludes people with decisive roles, and the thousands of collaborators are unrepresented. The 2013 prize already recognised the theory.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: the particle has been confirmed by both experiments and its properties measured to good precision. Recognition is arguably overdue except for the attribution problem.
uncertainties: Whether an individual-based allocation can be made fairly
Choice among the four credited leaders is unresolved

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and realisation of the quantum spin Hall effect and the topological insulator started a major field of condensed matter physics, with a new classification of phases and experimentally accessible protected edge and surface states. The ideas are original and the impact is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contribution; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Credit for the theory of HgTe and for the three-dimensional case (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hasan) is shared more broadly, so the trio is defensible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations, including ARPES and transport, make the field well established. Applications are still developing, but the foundational discovery is mature.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan, Fu, Moore and Balents remains contested
Practical impact has lagged the conceptual one

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of black holes in M87 and Sgr A*, using Earth-sized very-long-baseline interferometry at millimetre wavelengths. It is a striking observational achievement that tests strong-field gravity directly and is easy to communicate.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the VLBI development and the collaboration's formation and Zensus provided institutional leadership and instrumentation. The roles are real, but a collaboration of several hundred people makes a three-person division fraught, and imaging algorithm developers also made decisive contributions.
assessment.maturity: Two sources have been imaged and polarisation and multi-year data support the results. The interpretations of spin and accretion models are still evolving, so recognition may be slightly early.
uncertainties: Nobel recognition of black holes in 2020 may be seen as overlapping

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and hybrid pixel detectors transformed vertex and tracking detectors in particle physics and also spread to imaging and space instruments. They were essential for heavy-flavour physics and for the LHC experiments. The achievement is instrumentation rather than a discovery, but Charpak's 1992 prize is a precedent.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer introduced the planar process for silicon detectors, Parker developed microstrip devices and Heijne pioneered hybrid pixel detectors. This is a plausible three-way split, though other groups (for example CERN RD19 and the LAA project, and monolithic pixel developers) also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Entirely mature, with decades of use in several experiments and fields. The recognition is long overdue in timing terms.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to honour a technique rather than a discovery
Credit relative to other pixel and strip developers

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Self-amplified spontaneous emission X-ray free-electron lasers deliver femtosecond, intense coherent X-rays and enable new studies in structural biology, chemistry and ultrafast physics. The step from principle to working machines was a large and original accelerator achievement.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini is credited with the SASE concept for X-rays and LCLS leadership, Rossbach with TESLA test facility and FLASH and Ishikawa with SACLA. The allocation omits other prominent figures, such as Bonifacio and Kondratenko-Saldin, who established the SASE theory, so fairness is questionable.
assessment.maturity: Several facilities operate successfully and produce results at scale. The science enabled is mature, and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Early theory credit (Bonifacio, Kondratenko-Saldin) may undermine the proposed trio
Much of the impact is in applications rather than in fundamental physics

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays opens a new window on supermassive black-hole binaries and possibly early-universe physics. It is a long-baseline precision timing experiment of great ingenuity.
assessment.attribution: The evidence comes from NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA and IPTA, so credit is intrinsically shared among consortia. Manchester and Kramer represent the long-term pulsar timing programmes and Siemens the NANOGrav analysis, but McLaughlin and many others are equally central.
assessment.maturity: The evidence from several independent arrays is encouraging but near the 3-4 sigma level and the Hellings-Downs correlation and the astrophysical origin are not yet firmly established. A prize now would be premature.
uncertainties: Significance below discovery threshold in each array
Source of the signal (binaries versus new physics) is unresolved
Consortium credit does not map to three people
